```{r, echo = FALSE, message = FALSE}
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)
```

> **RETROSHEET DATA NOTICE**

> The information used here was obtained free of charge from and is copyrighted by Retrosheet. Interested parties may contact Retrosheet at 20 Sunset Rd., Newark, DE 19711.

Play-by-play events are what make Retrosheet special: no other freely available source describes every play of (nearly) every major league game for over a century. This article shows how to turn that notation into batting statistics, splits, and historical reconstructions with `parse_plays()`.

Because everything downloads from the web, the code chunks are not evaluated at build time; the tables shown are real outputs from the 2024 and 1954 postseasons.

## From notation to typed columns

`get_plays()` returns Retrosheet's raw event notation (`"S7/G56"`, `"64(1)3/GDP"`). `parse_plays()` interprets that notation and appends typed columns:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(retrosheetshow)
library(dplyr)

plays <- get_events(year = 2024, type = "post") |>
  get_plays() |>
  parse_plays()

plays |>
  select(event, event_type, is_hit, hit_value, trajectory, outs_on_play, rbi)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~event, ~event_type, ~is_hit, ~hit_value, ~trajectory, ~outs_on_play, ~rbi,
  "7/F7S", "generic_out", FALSE, 0L, "fly", 1L, 0L,
  "S7/G56", "single", TRUE, 1L, "ground", 0L, 0L,
  "K", "strikeout", FALSE, 0L, NA, 1L, 0L,
  "HR/F78XD.2-H;1-H", "home_run", TRUE, 4L, "fly", 0L, 3L
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Parsed play columns (selected 2024 postseason plays)")
```

The parser follows the published grammar at <https://www.retrosheet.org/eventfile.htm> and is validated against Chadwick's `cwevent`, the community reference implementation (see the package's test suite). A season of plays parses in a few seconds.

What happened, across the whole 2024 postseason:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plays |>
  count(event_type, sort = TRUE)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~event_type, ~n,
  "generic_out", 1459L,
  "strikeout", 739L,
  "no_play", 599L,
  "single", 443L,
  "walk", 309L,
  "double", 107L,
  "home_run", 98L,
  "stolen_base", 57L
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Most common events, 2024 postseason (top 8)")
```

(`no_play` records mark substitutions; filter them out or ignore them, since all their statistic columns are zero.)

## Batting lines from raw plays

The flag columns follow official scoring rules — sacrifices and catcher's interference are plate appearances but not at bats, walks never count as at bats — so slash lines are a single `summarize()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
batting <- plays |>
  summarize(
    pa = sum(is_plate_appearance),
    ab = sum(is_at_bat),
    h = sum(is_hit),
    hr = sum(event_type == "home_run"),
    rbi = sum(rbi),
    bb = sum(event_type %in% c("walk", "intentional_walk")),
    hbp = sum(event_type == "hit_by_pitch"),
    tb = sum(hit_value),
    sf = sum(is_sac_fly),
    .by = player_id
  ) |>
  mutate(
    avg = h / ab,
    obp = (h + bb + hbp) / (ab + bb + hbp + sf),
    slg = tb / ab
  )
```

Player IDs become names by joining the biographical database:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
players <- get_player_ids()

batting |>
  filter(pa >= 40) |>
  left_join(
    players |> select(player_id, first_name, last_name),
    by = "player_id"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(slg)) |>
  select(first_name, last_name, pa, h, hr, rbi, avg, obp, slg)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~first_name, ~last_name, ~pa, ~h, ~hr, ~rbi, ~avg, ~obp, ~slg,
  "Giancarlo", "Stanton", 62L, 15L, 7L, 16L, 0.273, 0.339, 0.709,
  "Mark", "Vientos", 58L, 18L, 5L, 14L, 0.327, 0.362, 0.636,
  "Juan", "Soto", 64L, 16L, 4L, 9L, 0.327, 0.469, 0.633,
  "Pete", "Alonso", 58L, 12L, 4L, 10L, 0.273, 0.431, 0.568,
  "Mookie", "Betts", 75L, 18L, 4L, 16L, 0.290, 0.387, 0.565
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "2024 postseason slugging leaders (minimum 40 PA)"
  )
```

## Situational splits

Each play carries the count when the event happened, so count-based splits need no extra data. Two strikes changes everything:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plays |>
  filter(is_plate_appearance, count != "??") |>
  mutate(two_strikes = substr(count, 2, 2) == "2") |>
  summarize(
    pa = n(),
    avg = sum(is_hit) / sum(is_at_bat),
    slg = sum(hit_value) / sum(is_at_bat),
    k_rate = mean(event_type == "strikeout"),
    .by = two_strikes
  )
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~two_strikes, ~pa, ~avg, ~slg, ~k_rate,
  FALSE, 1526L, 0.318, 0.513, 0,
  TRUE, 1740L, 0.156, 0.263, 0.425
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "2024 postseason hitting before vs. with two strikes"
  )
```

Other splits that work directly from the parsed columns: by inning, by home/visiting team (`team` is 0/1), bunts vs. full swings (`is_bunt`), or ball-in-play trajectory (`trajectory`, `hit_location`).

## A century of history: the 1954 World Series

Retrosheet's postseason coverage reaches back to 1903, and the same three lines of code work all the way down. Game 1 of the 1954 World Series contains perhaps the most famous defensive play ever made — Willie Mays' over-the-shoulder catch off Vic Wertz, with the game tied in the eighth:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plays_1954 <- get_events(year = 1954, type = "post") |>
  get_plays() |>
  parse_plays()

plays_1954 |>
  filter(game_id == "NY1195409290", inning == 8, team == 0, event != "NP") |>
  select(player_id, event, event_type, trajectory, hit_location, outs_on_play)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~player_id, ~event, ~event_type, ~trajectory, ~hit_location, ~outs_on_play,
  "dobyl101", "W", "walk", NA, NA, 0L,
  "rosea101", "S6.1-2", "single", NA, NA, 0L,
  "wertv101", "8/F8XD.2-3", "generic_out", "fly", "8XD", 1L,
  "mitcd101", "W.1-2", "walk", NA, NA, 0L,
  "poped101", "K/C", "strikeout", NA, NA, 1L,
  "hegaj101", "7", "generic_out", NA, NA, 1L
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Top of the 8th, 1954 World Series game 1")
```

The third row is The Catch: a fly out to center field, extra deep (`8XD`), with the runner from second only reaching third — a ball that leaves any other park. Two innings later the notation records how the game ended:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
plays_1954 |>
  filter(game_id == "NY1195409290", event_type == "home_run") |>
  select(player_id, inning, event, runs_on_play, rbi)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~player_id, ~inning, ~event, ~runs_on_play, ~rbi,
  "rhodd101", 10L, "HR/9D.2-H;1-H", 3L, 3L
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Dusty Rhodes' pinch-hit walk-off, 3 runs, 3 RBI")
```

Note the era differences: 1950s files rarely record counts, pitch sequences, or batted-ball trajectories, so those columns are `NA` when the source does not have them. Everything that is in the notation — events, outs, runs, RBI, advancement — parses the same in 1954 as in 2024.

## Game state: outs, runners, and score

`parse_plays()` reads one event string at a time, so it cannot know what the bases looked like when the play began. `track_game_state()` can: it replays each game's full record stream — plays, substitutions, and the automatic extra-inning runner — and returns every play with the situation it started from:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
states <- get_events(year = 2024, type = "post") |>
  track_game_state()
```

The most famous at-bat of the 2024 postseason, as the tracker sees it — Freddie Freeman stepping in with the World Series opener on the line:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
states |>
  filter(game_id == "LAN202410250", inning == 10, event_type == "home_run") |>
  select(player_id, event, outs_before,
         runner1_id, runner2_id, runner3_id, bat_score, fld_score)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~player_id, ~event, ~outs_before, ~runner1_id, ~runner2_id, ~runner3_id, ~bat_score, ~fld_score,
  "freef001", "HR/F9D.3-H;2-H;1-H", 2L, "bettm001", "edmat001", "taylc001", 2L, 3L
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Freeman's walk-off grand slam: two outs, bases loaded, down a run"
  )
```

Each play also carries the defense behind it: the pitcher, the fielder at every position, and the pitcher's running pitch count wherever Retrosheet has pitch sequences.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
states |>
  filter(game_id == "LAN202410250", inning == 10, event_type == "home_run") |>
  select(player_id, pitcher_id, pitch_count_before,
         fielder2_id, fielder6_id, fielder8_id)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~player_id, ~pitcher_id, ~pitch_count_before, ~fielder2_id, ~fielder6_id, ~fielder8_id,
  "freef001", "cortn001", 1L, "wella002", "volpa001", "judga001"
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Pitcher, pitch count, catcher, shortstop, and center fielder behind Freeman's grand slam"
  )
```

Nestor Cortes came in to face Shohei Ohtani and retired him on one pitch. The Yankees then walked Mookie Betts intentionally, which has taken no pitches since 2017, so Freeman's home run came on Cortes's second pitch of the night.

When a pitcher or batter is replaced in the middle of a count, the scoring rules can charge the outcome to the player who left: a walk goes to the departed pitcher if the batter was ahead 2-0, 2-1, or 3-anything, and a strikeout goes to the departed batter if he left with two strikes. `resp_pitcher_id` and `resp_batter_id` record who was charged. Two strikeouts in the 2025 postseason belong to batters who had already left the game:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
get_events(year = 2025, type = "post") |>
  track_game_state() |>
  filter(resp_batter_id != player_id) |>
  select(game_id, inning, player_id, resp_batter_id, pitches, event)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~game_id, ~inning, ~player_id, ~resp_batter_id, ~pitches, ~event,
  "LAN202510160", 7L, "perkb002", "chouj001", "SS.F.FBFBS", "K",
  "LAN202510010", 8L, "andum001", "bensw001", "FCFB..S", "K"
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Strikeouts charged to the batter who left with two strikes, 2025 postseason"
  )
```

State columns are validated against Chadwick's `cwevent` the same way the parser is: on the golden files and in full-season cross-checks of 1954, 2024, and 2025, the outs, scores, runners, pitcher, fielders, and responsible pitcher and batter agreed on every one of ~480,000 events. Knowing the out count also lets `track_game_state()` apply the one scoring rule the string-level parser cannot — no RBI for a runner from third scoring on an error with two outs — so its `rbi` column is exact.

## Linking to Statcast and other sources

Every player in these tables is identified by Retrosheet ID. Other sources use their own: Statcast's pitch-tracking data identifies batters and pitchers by MLBAM ID, the ID system of MLB Advanced Media. `get_chadwick_register()` maps one to the other, along with Baseball-Reference and FanGraphs IDs, using the Chadwick Baseball Bureau's register of people in baseball:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
ids <- get_chadwick_register()

states |>
  filter(game_id == "LAN202410250", inning == 10, event_type == "home_run") |>
  select(player_id, pitcher_id) |>
  left_join(
    select(ids, player_id = key_retro, batter_mlbam = key_mlbam),
    by = "player_id"
  ) |>
  left_join(
    select(ids, pitcher_id = key_retro, pitcher_mlbam = key_mlbam),
    by = "pitcher_id"
  )
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~player_id, ~pitcher_id, ~batter_mlbam, ~pitcher_mlbam,
  "freef001", "cortn001", 518692L, 641482L
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Freeman's grand slam, with the MLBAM IDs Statcast uses")
```

With those IDs, the same plate appearance can be matched in Statcast's pitch-by-pitch data. The register is a single download of about 28 MB, cached like everything else. Chadwick updates it periodically, and `get_chadwick_register(refresh = TRUE)` replaces the cached copy with the current version.

## Run expectancy

With base-out states attached, the classic RE24 matrix is a dozen lines: for each play, count the runs scored from that point to the end of the half-inning, then average by starting state.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
states <- get_events(year = 2024) |>
  track_game_state()

re24 <- states |>
  mutate(
    bases = paste0(
      if_else(is.na(runner1_id), "-", "1"),
      if_else(is.na(runner2_id), "-", "2"),
      if_else(is.na(runner3_id), "-", "3")
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    runs_rest = rev(cumsum(rev(runs_on_play))),
    complete = sum(outs_on_play) == 3,
    .by = c(game_id, inning, team)
  ) |>
  filter(complete) |>
  summarize(re = mean(runs_rest), .by = c(bases, outs_before))

re24 |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    id_cols = bases, names_from = outs_before,
    values_from = re, names_prefix = "outs_"
  ) |>
  arrange(bases)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~bases, ~outs_0, ~outs_1, ~outs_2,
  "---", 0.48, 0.25, 0.09,
  "--3", 1.36, 0.93, 0.34,
  "-2-", 1.08, 0.65, 0.33,
  "-23", 1.98, 1.37, 0.58,
  "1--", 0.89, 0.52, 0.22,
  "1-3", 1.85, 1.17, 0.48,
  "12-", 1.46, 0.92, 0.43,
  "123", 2.25, 1.61, 0.80
) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    caption = "Run expectancy by base-out state, 2024 regular season"
  )
```

Freeman's grand slam, in these terms: bases loaded with two outs is worth 0.80 expected runs, and he delivered four. The same state table is the foundation for RE24 batting value, stolen-base break-even rates, and bunting analysis — all now a `summarize()` away.

## What the string-level parser alone cannot know

If you use `parse_plays()` without `track_game_state()`, keep in mind:

* `runner1_dest`, `runner2_dest`, and `runner3_dest` are `NA` when the play does not mention that runner — a runner who holds is indistinguishable from an empty base. `track_game_state()` resolves this with its `runner*_id` columns.
* The `rbi` column defaults to crediting the rule 9.04(a)(3) edge case (runner from third scoring on an error with two outs); `track_game_state()` corrects it. In two full validation seasons this affected 2 plays in about 283,000.
